title: Read the case before your role
hook: Would you judge the same facts differently after learning which side you represent?

knows: basic arithmetic and reading a small table
doesNotKnow: Contrast evaluation before role assignment with self-serving interpretation afterward.

misconception: The quantities in this case can be combined without checking their reference, denominator, or information boundary.
objective: Contrast evaluation before role assignment with self-serving interpretation afterward.
keyState: Both complete computed cases are visible as retained observations; the question-case picture survives Reset.

claims.text: A toy reader weights evidence scores four and zero equally. What is the combined score before taking a side? Toy inputs A=[4, 0, 1, 1]; B=[4, 0, 2, 1].
claims.source: Local explicit hypothetical assumptions in spec.ts and model.ts; not participant measurements.

claims.text: Computed results: [[2, 1, 1], [2.6666666666666665, 2, 1]]. Labels: Weighted score, Favor weight, Other weight.
claims.source: compute() in the lesson-local model.ts; finite numeric operations over the explicit inputs.

claims.text: The comparison changes evidence weights after role assignment while keeping the facts fixed. That is one explicit model of self-serving interpretation. It does not show that every negotiator applies these weights or that role timing is the only cause.
claims.source: The two controlled cases in spec.ts; scope limited to these toy inputs and displayed model rule.

claims.text: A new toy case uses Favorable score=4, Other score=0, Favor weight=2, Other weight=1. What is Weighted score? Answer: 2.667.
claims.source: compute() applied to the contrasting new input case; source list is an idea pointer only.

recall.question: A new toy case uses Favorable score=4, Other score=0, Favor weight=2, Other weight=1. What is Weighted score?
recall.why: Applying the stated toy rule to the new inputs gives 2.667. The result depends on these assumptions; it is not a universal behavioral response.

sourceProvenance.text: When negotiators read case facts before learning their role, settlements came much more easily than when they knew their side first (Babcock, Loewenstein, Issacharoff & Camerer, 1995).
sourceProvenance.caveat: Original list says figures are approximate and papers were not individually rechecked. No empirical source is verified by this build.

meaningfulDifference: Contrast evaluation before role assignment with self-serving interpretation afterward.
